transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Well, to be honest, it was mostly my wife’s idea for me to come in. See, I’m not working these days, so I’m around the house a lot, and we’ve been helping out my cousin quite a bit lately. He’s got all these different appointments, needs rides all over town, physical therapy, that sort of thing. My wife is the one who usually coordinates all his schedule stuff, because she's just better at keeping track of it all. 

And, well, what really brought me in is that she’ll be standing right there in the kitchen—maybe wiping down the counters or something—and she'll be telling me all about my cousin’s appointments or when he needs a ride... and I’m looking right at her. I mean, I’m making direct eye contact, I'm nodding, I really think I'm paying attention to the conversation. But then, maybe a minute later, she'll ask me to confirm the time I need to pick him up, and I just... I realize I didn’t actually take in half of what she said. The words just sort of evaporated into thin air. 

She gets so frustrated, which I completely understand, because she thinks I'm just ignoring her or that I don't care about helping my cousin, but I really am trying to listen. It's just that it keeps happening, especially with these rides and schedules, and she finally told me I had to come see a doctor about it because she's just at her wit's end having to repeat herself all the time. So, that's really what started all this.
Has this kind of trouble focusing and 'losing' conversations been something you've dealt with since you were a kid, or is this a new pattern that's really only shown up recently?

Well, you know, my wife actually asked me that exact same thing the other day when she finally told me to make this appointment. And I had to really stop and think about it, because when you're my age—I'm 59 now—you sort of just get used to how your brain works, right? You just think, 'well, that's just how I am.' But no, to answer your question, this isn't a new thing at all. Not by a long shot. 

In fact, if I really think back on it, it goes all the way back to when I was just a little kid. I mean, definitely before I was even 12 years old, way back in grade school. I can still vividly picture those old wooden desks we had back then, the kind where the whole top lifts up on a hinge? My parents used to go to those parent-teacher conferences every fall, and it was almost comical because it was the exact same story every single year, no matter who the teacher was. They would sit my folks down and say, you know, 'Oh, he’s a very bright boy, he has so much potential,' but then they’d immediately follow it up with how I was just constantly daydreaming. 

I'd be staring out the window watching a bird or just completely lost in my own world while the teacher was standing right at the chalkboard talking... which, now that I say it out loud, sounds exactly like what happens with my wife in the kitchen. And my desk was a disaster. I was always, always leaving my homework stuffed way in the back of my desk. I'd do the work, or at least I'd mean to do it, and then I'd just completely forget it was sitting right there in the dark. The teachers were constantly having to walk down the aisle and tap on my desk or call my name just to give me reminders to finish the classwork that was sitting right in front of my face. 

So, yeah, it's definitely not a new pattern. It’s just... well, it’s always been this way. I guess it's just that now it's causing real friction with my wife and my cousin's schedule, whereas back then it was just Mrs. Gable in the fourth grade getting frustrated with me for not finishing my spelling worksheets, you know? But the feeling of just losing the thread of what's going on around me, that's been there my whole life.
Aside from these attention lapses, have you been feeling unusually worried, anxious, sad, or low in energy recently?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, sure, nobody likes having their spouse upset with them, so I get a little tense right in the moment when she's frustrated with me, but... no, I'm not unusually worried or sad or anything like that. 

Actually, since I left the workforce—I took a sort of early out a little while back, which is why I'm around the house so much now—I've generally been in pretty good spirits. I don't really sit around worrying or feeling down. And my energy is actually pretty good for a guy pushing sixty! Like, just the other day, I was out in the garage for probably four or five hours straight, just tinkering with this old lawnmower of ours. I was trying to get the carburetor cleaned out, because, well, you know how those things get all gunked up if you leave the gas in them over the winter without putting that stabilizer in. I meant to put it in last fall, but it just slipped my mind. Anyway, if I was depressed or low on energy, I definitely wouldn't have the drive to be out there pulling small engines apart, right? I just get caught up in whatever I'm doing. 

So, yeah, physically and emotionally, I feel fine. I sleep well, my appetite is good. I do try not to watch too much of the evening news because, well, that'll make anybody feel a little sad these days with how crazy the world is, so I just stick to the morning paper and leave it at that. But in my own day-to-day life? No, I'm perfectly content. It really is just this... this frustrating thing where my brain just seems to hit a blank wall when she's giving me instructions. That's the only real dark cloud, just feeling guilty that I'm making things harder for her and my cousin when I drop the ball. But as far as my actual mood and energy go, no, I'm doing just fine.
